opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is a business decision and part of it is a kind of philosophical bet. From a business point of view, it makes complete sense. If you can have one model that you train once at enormous cost and then everybody uses it for everything, from writing poetry to writing code to planning their vacation, that's a very attractive proposition. You amortize the cost, you have one product, one API, and you keep scaling it.

The philosophical bet is a sort of extreme reading of the bitter lesson: that generality plus scale will eventually subsume everything, so you don't need specialized reasoners, verifiers, or domain models. Just make the big thing bigger and train it on more stuff, and the reasoning will emerge.

My concern, and I've been saying this for a while, is that generality and guarantees tend to pull in opposite directions. These models are wonderful at what I call approximate retrieval. They're very good at generating plausible candidates in almost any domain. But plausible is not the same as correct. When you look at things like planning, where there are actual constraints and you can check whether a plan works, you find the models generate things that look right but often aren't. If you change the names of the objects, as we did in our obfuscated Blocksworld experiments, performance drops dramatically, which tells you something about what's actually going on inside.

So I don't think the right architecture is one monolithic model that does everything end to end. I think the more sensible picture is what we've called LLM-Modulo: you use the LLM as a great idea generator, a great source of guesses, and you put it in a loop with external verifiers and critics, some of which might be symbolic, some might be simulators, some might be humans, that actually check correctness. The generality lives in the generator; the guarantees come from the verifiers.

Interestingly, if you look at what has happened with the reasoning models, the o1-style things, they've effectively started to move in that direction, though somewhat quietly. They generate lots of candidate traces and use some form of verification or learned evaluation during training and sometimes inference. So even within the single-model story, there's a recognition that pure autoregressive generation isn't enough. The question is whether you bake all of that inside one opaque box, or whether you make the verification explicit and modular, so you can actually trust and inspect what comes out. I lean pretty strongly toward the latter, especially for anything safety-critical.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes business incentives and a bet on generality and scale, but does not connect that preference to humans having one brain.

r002.rationale: The candidate advocates modular verification, but says nothing about whether AI must reproduce the brain’s mechanisms.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not speculate that building AI could reveal how the brain works.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not distinguish AI as a neuroscience research tool from AI as an explanation of brain function.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to understand it partly as a business decision and partly as a kind of ideological commitment, and the two reinforce each other. The business part is easy: if you're OpenAI, you want one thing that everybody uses for everything. One model, one API, one subscription. The moment you admit that different tasks might need different kinds of systems, you've opened the door to a world where nobody needs you in particular. So there's a strong incentive to say the general model is the answer to everything.

The ideological part is more interesting to me. There's this deep belief, which goes back to the early days of AI really, that intelligence is one thing, and if you just get enough of it, everything else falls out. The LLM folks have essentially inherited that, except now the one thing is "scale." Feed it more data, make it bigger, and planning, reasoning, verification, all of it will emerge. And to be fair, they've been surprised on the upside more than once, so I understand why they keep betting that way.

But my own view has been that this conflates two very different things. Large language models are phenomenal at what I'd call approximate retrieval. They are extraordinary at producing plausible-looking completions given everything they've absorbed. What they are not, natively, is a system that can guarantee correctness. When you need a plan that actually works, when you need a proof that actually holds, you need verification, and verification is a fundamentally different computation from generation. You can't get it by just making the generator bigger.

So what I find a little amusing is that even OpenAI, in practice, isn't really shipping a single monolithic model. Look at what they've done with the reasoning models. There's a generator, there's some kind of search or sampling, there's a verifier or a reward model in the loop somewhere. That's not one model. That's a system. They call it one model because that's the product story, but architecturally they've conceded the point. They've essentially built what I've been calling an LLM-Modulo framework, with the LLM producing candidates and something else doing the checking. They just put it all behind one name.

So I'd put it this way: the preference for a single general-purpose model is real at the level of marketing and worldview, but the engineering reality is drifting toward exactly the kind of hybrid systems that some of us have been arguing for. The question is whether they'll ever say that out loud, because admitting it undermines the "just scale it" story that the whole valuation rests on.

r001.rationale: The response links the preference to a belief that intelligence is one thing, but does not suggest an analogy with humans having one brain.

r002.rationale: The response discusses hybrid AI systems, but says nothing about whether AI must reproduce the brain’s mechanisms.

r003.rationale: It discusses scale and OpenAI’s worldview, but does not connect building AI with learning how the brain works.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss neuroscience research or distinguish its use of AI from treating AI as an explanation of the brain.

astra-6.text:
I think the attraction is that you have one model that can be applied to many different tasks through the same interface. That’s a very appealing goal. But we should distinguish a general-purpose model from a general-purpose intelligent system. Those are not necessarily the same thing.

A system can have broad capabilities precisely because it brings together different components. You might have a language model proposing possibilities, a planner working out actions, and a verifier checking whether a proposed solution actually satisfies the constraints. The user could experience all of that as one assistant. There’s no requirement that everything underneath be one model.

So my question would be: is the commitment to generality, or is it to a particular architecture for achieving generality? I’m sympathetic to the first. The second should be an empirical question. If combining a model with other forms of reasoning gives you more reliable behavior, then that’s something we should embrace.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a single model versus a system of components, but does not connect OpenAI’s preference to an analogy with the human brain.

r002.rationale: It says a general system can combine different components, but does not state that AI need not reproduce the brain’s mechanisms.

r003.rationale: The response does not speculate that building AI could reveal how the brain works.

r004.rationale: It makes no distinction between AI as a neuroscience tool and AI as an explanation of brain function.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two things: a single interface that people can use for many different tasks, and a single model that actually does everything. The first is very attractive. You don’t want users to have to figure out which of twenty systems they should talk to. But that doesn’t mean that, underneath that interface, the same model should be doing all the work.

You could have a general-purpose model that understands the request and then calls a planner, a solver, or some other specialized tool. From the user’s perspective, it’s still one assistant. Architecturally, it’s a collection of capabilities.

So my question would be: is the preference for a single model a useful engineering hypothesis, or is it becoming a commitment that everything must emerge from that model? Those are very different positions. Generality at the interface doesn’t require uniformity underneath.
